profiles.name: Alice Frost
profiles.excerpt: Alice Frost was a foundational American radio actress, from the Mercury Theatre to long-running leads on Big Sister and Mr. and Mrs. North; one isolated Lux sponsor tag is not enough to classify her as a commercial performer.
profiles.bio_html:
Alice Frost built the kind of career that demonstrates how important radio could be to an actor long before television. Born in Minnesota in 1910, she worked on stage and became an inaugural member of Orson Welles’s Mercury Theatre company, then moved into some of network radio’s most durable female leads.

Frost played Ruth Evans in Big Sister and later became especially identified with Pamela North on Mr. and Mrs. North, a role she held for nearly a decade. GRH’s surviving dramatic holdings capture only part of that much larger career, including The Shadow, The Clock, Inner Sanctum, Mercury Theatre and other anthologies.

The detailed GRH index contains one Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman tag for Frost. Because a single isolated sponsor tag does not establish a separate commercial career, GRH preserves the credit for verification but does not publicly classify her under Commercial Voices & Sponsor Performers.

profiles.name: Noreen Gammill
profiles.excerpt: Noreen Gammill was an early radio monologist, writer and versatile character actress whose later Lux work also placed her inside the sponsor presentation of network drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Noreen Gammill was already experimenting with radio performance in the medium’s early years. Period profiles describe her broadcasting in Kansas City around 1920, performing one-act plays in which she supplied multiple characters and accents from memory. She later moved to Los Angeles, wrote, performed sketches and became known for a broad range of dialect voices.

That versatility carried into network radio, animation and later television. Gammill became the original Mrs. Martha Conklin on Our Miss Brooks and also supplied the voice of Catty the Elephant in Disney’s Dumbo. GRH preserves her across prestige drama, university adaptations, mystery and comedy.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 28 Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman/performer credits, nine NBC University Theater performances, six Let George Do It appearances and additional work on Dr. Christian, The Great Gildersleeve, Lights Out and other programs. The Lux sponsor work fits a career already built on vocal versatility.

profiles.name: John Gibson
profiles.excerpt: John Gibson became radio’s Ethelbert the bartender on Casey, Crime Photographer, the steady listener inside the Blue Note Café who heard Casey retell each week’s case.
profiles.bio_html:
John Gibson’s defining radio role was Ethelbert, the bartender at the Blue Note Café on Casey, Crime Photographer. The character was structurally important even when he was not solving the crime: Casey’s return to the bar gave the series a recurring home base where the photographer could recount or reflect on the week’s investigation.

Gibson stayed with the role through the radio run and even carried Ethelbert into the early television adaptation. His broader radio career also included science fiction, experimental drama and anthology work. GRH’s data additionally preserves commercial-spokesman tags on Calling All Cars, showing a smaller sponsor-facing side of the same working career.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 69 Casey, Crime Photographer performances, nine each on Theater Five and X Minus One, eight Columbia Workshop appearances and seven Calling All Cars commercial-spokesman/performer credits. GRH therefore keeps sponsor performance as a secondary facet beside the much larger Ethelbert legacy.

profiles.name: Gloria Gordon
profiles.excerpt: Gloria Gordon was a regular Lux Radio Theatre supporting actress whose sponsor-facing work sat beside comedy, mystery and musical-radio roles.
profiles.bio_html:
Gloria Gordon belonged to the dependable supporting company around Hollywood network radio. Period radio histories list her among the regular voices heard on Lux Radio Theatre, where experienced actors filled secondary roles around the week’s film stars and kept large adaptations moving efficiently.

GRH’s records also place Gordon on The Halls of Ivy, The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show, The Whistler, The Railroad Hour and Broadway Is My Beat. The Lux material repeatedly includes commercial-spokesman tags, showing that sponsor presentation was part of the flexibility expected from her.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman/performer credits, 11 Halls of Ivy performances and smaller holdings across the other series. Her profile therefore emphasizes the radio repertory system rather than a single signature character.

profiles.name: Paul Huber
profiles.excerpt: Paul Huber became a recurring commercial voice of The Shadow, speaking for Blue Coal as the sponsor character John Barclay across dozens of broadcasts.
profiles.bio_html:
Paul Huber’s most substantial surviving radio identity is commercial rather than dramatic. On The Shadow, Mutual’s long-running mystery series sponsored by Blue Coal, Huber repeatedly appeared as the commercial spokesman identified as “John Barclay.”

The sponsor character mattered because The Shadow was built inside the economics of commercial radio. Blue Coal’s message was not an unrelated spot inserted after the program. The commercial voice was part of the familiar weekly frame surrounding Lamont Cranston, Margot Lane, the announcer and the organ music, and listeners heard the same sponsor persona return from episode to episode.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 78 The Shadow commercial-spokesman/performer-tagged credits for Huber. That sustained run makes him one of the clearest examples in the GRH archive of a person whose radio biography genuinely belongs in Commercial Voices & Sponsor Performers.

profiles.name: David Kerman
profiles.excerpt: David Kerman was a recurring Lux Radio Theatre supporting actor whose sponsor work continued alongside later dramatic appearances on Theater Five and other anthologies.
profiles.bio_html:
David Kerman is preserved most strongly through Lux Radio Theatre, where cast records show him doubling in supporting roles around major Hollywood stars. That kind of work required speed and vocal distinction because a supporting actor might play more than one small part inside the same adaptation.

GRH’s Lux records also carry commercial-spokesman tags for Kerman, extending the same vocal utility into sponsor material. He later remained active enough to appear on Theater Five, Dr. Christian, The Chase and X Minus One, connecting classic Hollywood radio with the medium’s later anthology years.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits and 13 Theater Five performances, plus smaller appearances elsewhere. GRH keeps the biography centered on that verified working career because personal documentation is limited.

profiles.name: John Lake
profiles.excerpt: John Lake was one of Lux Radio Theatre’s recurring studio voices, appearing in both supporting dramatic work and the sponsor presentation woven through the weekly anthology.
profiles.bio_html:
John Lake survives in the GRH record chiefly through Lux Radio Theatre. Like many members of the anthology’s regular studio company, he worked behind the celebrity billing that dominated advertisements for the program.

His credits carry both performer and commercial-spokesman roles. That combination is historically useful because it shows how radio actors could be deployed across the supposedly separate worlds of story and advertising within the same live production.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits for Lake. With little reliable personal biography currently available, GRH does not pad the page beyond what those repeated broadcasts can establish.

profiles.name: Mary Lansing
profiles.excerpt: Mary Lansing built a durable West Coast radio career across mystery, westerns and comedy, while Lux Radio Theatre also used her repeatedly in sponsor-facing work.
profiles.bio_html:
Mary Lansing was a New Orleans-born actress who worked extensively in radio before becoming a familiar television character player. Radio connected her to a large circle of Los Angeles performers, including actor Frank Nelson, whom she met while both were working in broadcasting.

Her GRH record shows unusual breadth: The Whistler, Gunsmoke, Fibber McGee and Molly, Jeff Regan, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, Nero Wolfe and other programs. On Lux Radio Theatre, she also appears under commercial-spokesman and commercial-spokeswoman tags, adding sponsor presentation to an already broad acting career.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits, 17 The Whistler performances, six Gunsmoke appearances and multiple detective and comedy credits. GRH therefore treats the sponsor work as one documented specialty inside a much larger repertory career.

profiles.name: Bobby Larson
profiles.excerpt: Bobby Larson was a recurring Lux Radio Theatre studio voice whose preserved work crossed supporting performance and sponsor presentation.
profiles.bio_html:
Bobby Larson is another performer whose GRH biography is strongest when it stays close to the surviving broadcast record. His current archive identity is concentrated in Lux Radio Theatre, where weekly film adaptations depended on a supporting company far larger than the stars named in newspaper advertising.

Larson’s credits combine performer and commercial-spokesman roles. That repeated overlap indicates practical studio versatility rather than a one-time metadata accident: the same voice could fill a small dramatic role and then help deliver the sponsor material that financed the broadcast.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits for Bobby Larson. Until stronger personal sources emerge, GRH keeps the page centered on that verifiable work.

profiles.name: Herb Lytton
profiles.excerpt: Herb Lytton was a recurring West Coast mystery actor whose Whistler work dominates his GRH record, with additional sponsor-facing appearances on Lux Radio Theatre.
profiles.bio_html:
Herb Lytton appears in Golden Radio Hour primarily as a West Coast dramatic actor, especially in The Whistler. The anthology’s crime stories depended on a rotating repertory of actors who could establish ordinary, believable people quickly before the plot turned toward guilt, violence or reversal.

Lytton also appeared on Lux Radio Theatre, where GRH’s records carry both performer and commercial-spokesman tags. He later turns up on Screen Directors Playhouse and Roy Rogers, showing that his radio work was not confined to one genre.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 23 The Whistler performances, six Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits and smaller holdings elsewhere. GRH keeps commercial work as a secondary facet of a career whose strongest preserved identity is dramatic repertory.

profiles.name: Myra Marsh
profiles.excerpt: Myra Marsh moved between radio mothers, neighbors and authority figures before a later film and television career, with Lux Radio Theatre also using her in sponsor-facing work.
profiles.bio_html:
Myra Marsh was born in Maine in 1894 and became a character actress whose mature screen and television roles often drew on the same grounded vocal presence radio had already used. Her radio work ranged across family comedy, small-town drama, literary anthology and mystery.

GRH preserves Marsh on A Date with Judy, Dr. Christian, Fibber McGee and Molly, The Railroad Hour, Let George Do It, NBC University Theater and Night Beat. Her Lux Radio Theatre records also include commercial-spokesman tags, adding sponsor presentation to the character work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven appearances each on A Date with Judy and Dr. Christian, five Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits and smaller holdings across the other series. GRH treats those sponsor credits as a secondary but verified part of her radio career.
